summary:
PlanetPulse: NASA Earth System Trend Detective is a web platform that helps users judge whether a long-term change in NASA climate data is statistically real or just natural variability. Many dashboards plot a line and leave interpretation to the viewer. This one tests it.

Users pick a variable, choose a location on an interactive 3D globe or from presets such as Lucknow and Svalbard, and set a year range. The app pulls monthly point records from the NASA POWER API for air temperature, precipitation, humidity and soil wetness, filters missing-data flags without interpolation, and runs Mann-Kendall tests, Theil-Sen slopes and linear regression with 95% confidence bounds. Seasonal cycles can be removed with a toggle. A FastAPI service using SciPy and PyMannKendall performs the statistics, and a built-in JavaScript engine takes over if the service is unreachable. The dashboard returns a plain-language verdict, NASA GIBS satellite imagery, multi-region comparison, and CSV and PDF exports.

Rank-based tests suit noisy climate records because they need no normality assumption and resist outliers. By turning raw archives into a guided, evidence-based workflow, the platform lets students and early-stage analysts separate signal from noise before drawing conclusions
details:
Project Title: PlanetPulse - NASA Earth Detective

What it Does and How it Works

PlanetPulse is an advanced, full-stack scientific analysis and visualization platform designed to monitor, analyze, and predict Earth systems trends using NASA satellite imagery and datasets. It acts as an interactive "Earth Detective," bridging the gap between raw, complex geospatial data and actionable climate intelligence.

How it works:

  1. Data Ingestion: The platform seamlessly connects to multiple NASA data pipelines (such as NASA POWER and Earth Observation data) via a custom datasetProvider and nasa_resources.py backend service.
  2. Statistical Processing: Once raw data is fetched, it is passed through a robust FastAPI Python backend. Custom statistical engines (seasonal_analysis.py and trend_analyzer.py) decompose time-series data, filter out noise, and identify significant seasonal shifts or climate anomalies.
  3. Interactive Visualization: The processed intelligence is sent to a Next.js frontend where it is mapped onto an interactive WebGL 3D Earth visualization (EarthGlobe.js). High-resolution textures (atmospheric, cloud, and specular maps) allow users to visually pinpoint data across the globe.
  4. AI-Assisted Investigation: An integrated AI Assistant (AiAssistantModal.js) acts as a co-pilot, helping users query complex geospatial trends, interpret statistical anomalies, and generate plain-language summaries of the data presented in the TimeSeriesChart and VerdictCard components.

Benefits of the Project

  • Democratization of Climate Data: It transforms terabytes of intimidating, raw NASA JSON/CSV payloads into intuitive, visually engaging dashboards that require zero coding or data science expertise to understand.
  • Rapid Anomaly Detection: By automating the statistical decomposition of time-series data, researchers and students can instantly spot concerning trends (like unprecedented temperature spikes or vegetation loss) rather than spending hours cleaning and plotting data manually.
  • Contextual Intelligence: Instead of just showing graphs, the VerdictCard component and the AI Assistant provide definitive, context-aware conclusions about what the data actually means for a specific region.

Intended Impact

The core impact of PlanetPulse is to empower environmental decision-making and climate education at all levels. By making Earth's vital signs highly visible and easy to interrogate, the project aims to equip policymakers, environmental researchers, educators, and citizen scientists with the evidence they need to advocate for sustainability. It lowers the barrier to entry for climate science, turning passive observers into active "Earth Detectives" who can independently verify and explore the impacts of global change.

Tech Stack: Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software

PlanetPulse was built using a decoupled, modern web architecture to ensure high performance and scalability:

  • Frontend (User Interface & 3D WebGL):

    • Framework: Next.js (App Router) and React.
    • Languages: JavaScript / JSX, HTML5, CSS3.
    • Styling: Tailwind CSS for rapid, responsive UI design.
    • Visualization: WebGL/Three.js (powering the EarthGlobe.js component with 2K/4K textures for specular, cloud, and atmospheric rendering).
    • Package Management: pnpm in a workspace configuration.
    • Framework: FastAPI for high-performance, asynchronous API routing.
    • Language: Python 3.10+.
    • Analysis Libraries: Built-in Python statistical modules, augmented by custom logic in trend_analyzer.py and data_processor.py.
    • Testing: Pytest suite (test_statistical_engine.py) to ensure scientific and mathematical accuracy.
    • Database: MongoDB (mongodb.js) for storing user configurations, investigation histories, and cached reports.
    • External APIs: NASA POWER API, NASA Earth Imagery API, and an AI Provider API for the assistant routes.
    • Hosting: Vercel (configured via vercel.json for both frontend edge delivery and backend serverless function execution).

How the Project is Creative

PlanetPulse steps away from the traditional, dry "dashboard and spreadsheet" approach to scientific data. The creativity lies in its gamified, investigative UI—positioning the user as an "Earth Detective." By marrying rigorous backend statistical math with a visually stunning, tactile 3D globe, it creates an immersive experience. Furthermore, integrating a contextual AI Assistant directly into the workflow transforms the platform from a simple data viewer into an active research partner that can converse with the user about the visual evidence they are looking at.

Factors the Team Considered During Development

  • Performance vs. Visual Fidelity: Rendering a 3D globe with live data in the browser can be resource-intensive. We carefully balanced texture resolutions (earth_atmos_2048.jpg, earth_clouds_1024.png) and optimized the React component lifecycle to ensure smooth 60fps rendering without crashing lower-end hardware.
  • Scientific Accuracy: When dealing with climate data, misleading visualizations can be dangerous. We prioritized the development of a dedicated test_statistical_engine.py to ensure that our trend lines, seasonal decompositions, and anomaly flags were mathematically sound before reaching the UI.
  • API Rate Limiting & Reliability: NASA's public endpoints can be subject to rate limits and latency. We structured our backend to handle asynchronous requests gracefully, employing data processors that clean, normalize, and cache data to ensure the frontend remains snappy even if upstream APIs are slow.
  • Modularity for Future Expansion: The frontend is strictly componentized (TimeSeriesChart, VerdictCard, SatelliteImageryViewer), and the backend separates routes from core services. This modular architecture was designed intentionally so that integrating new datasets (like ESA Copernicus or NOAA) in the future requires minimal refactoring.
